blocks.text: Every client that talks to a server eventually hits a failure.
Some failures are just noise, a blip that clears up on its own if you try again.
Others are permanent, and retrying them only wastes time while hiding a real problem.
1. What a Retry Actually Is

blocks.alt: A failed request gets classified before any retry happens

blocks.text: A retry is simply the client trying the same request again after it failed.
The interesting part is not the trying again, it is deciding when that is a good idea.
Retry logic is really a small decision engine wrapped around an ordinary request.
Get that decision wrong and a client either gives up too early or hammers a server that needed a moment to recover.
2. Failures Worth Retrying: The Transient Network Blip
A transient failure is temporary by nature, it tends to clear up on its own within seconds.
A dropped packet, a brief timeout, or a server restarting mid request usually resolves if the client just tries again.
The connection itself may already be healthy again by the time a retry goes out.
3. Failures Not Worth Retrying: A Permission Error
A permission error means the server understood the request perfectly and still said no.
Retrying the exact same request gets the exact same no, every single time.
Nothing about waiting a second and trying again changes who is allowed to do what.
Retrying here just delays telling the user or the agent the thing it actually needs to know.
4. Failures Not Worth Retrying: A Malformed Request
A malformed request is broken on the client side, a missing field, a wrong type, or bad syntax.
Sending that same broken request again produces the same rejection again.
The fix here is correcting the request, not waiting and resending it unchanged.
5. Telling Transient and Permanent Failures Apart

blocks.alt: A transient failure is compared against a permanent failure

blocks.text: Most transports carry enough information to classify a failure without guessing.
A network level timeout or a connection reset is a strong signal of something transient.
An explicit error code like a permission denial or a validation failure is a strong signal of something permanent.

blocks.text: When in doubt, treat an error as not retryable, a skipped retry is cheaper than one that repeats a harmful action.
6. Why Retrying Immediately Is a Bad Idea

blocks.alt: An immediate retry can pile onto an already struggling server

blocks.text: Trying again the instant a request fails feels natural, but it rarely helps a struggling server.
A server that is overloaded gets no relief if every failed client fires right back at it.
A short pause before the first retry already changes the outcome for the better.
7. Exponential Backoff

blocks.alt: Each retry attempt waits longer than the one before it

blocks.text: Exponential backoff waits longer after each failed attempt instead of using a fixed delay every time.
The first retry might wait about one second, the next about two seconds, then four, then eight.
This gives a struggling server real breathing room instead of a wall of instant retries.
A maximum delay cap keeps that doubling from growing into an unreasonably long wait.
8. Why Jitter Matters

blocks.alt: Many clients retrying at the same instant is spread apart with jitter

blocks.text: If many clients fail at the same moment and all back off on the exact same schedule, they end up retrying together anyway.
That synchronized retry is sometimes called a thundering herd, and it can hit a recovering server just as hard as no backoff at all.
Jitter adds a small random amount to each delay so retries spread out instead of clustering.

items: Add jitter as a random fraction of the current delay, not a fixed extra amount.
Keep the randomness small enough that the overall backoff trend still holds.
Recompute jitter fresh on every attempt, never reuse the same random value twice.

blocks.text: 9. A Retry Function With Backoff and Jitter
Here is a small retry wrapper that combines a retryable check, exponential backoff, jitter, and a maximum attempt count.
Notice the retryable check runs first, backoff and jitter only apply once a failure has already passed that check.
The cap on delay and the cap on attempts are two separate limits, and this function honors both of them.
10. Setting a Maximum Retry Count

blocks.alt: Attempts under the maximum keep retrying while attempts over it stop

blocks.text: Retrying forever is never the right default, a client needs a hard stop.
Once the cap is hit, the client should fail clearly rather than hang silently in the background.

blocks.title: Pick a cap on purpose
blocks.content: A quick lookup might allow three attempts, a background sync might allow more, but every operation should have some finite cap chosen deliberately, not left as an accident of the code.

blocks.text: 11. What Happens When the Cap Is Reached
Hitting the cap is not a bug, it is the retry logic doing exactly its job.
The client should surface a clear final error, not swallow the failure quietly.
Whatever called the retrying function needs enough information to decide what happens next.
12. Retrying at the Request Level vs the Connection Level

blocks.alt: Retrying at the request level is compared against retrying at the connection level

blocks.text: Not every retry is about a single request, sometimes the entire connection is gone.
A request level retry just resends one call over a connection that is already working.
A connection level retry has to reestablish the connection itself before anything else can happen.

blocks.text: 13. Connecting Back to Reconnection Strategies
The Transport Mechanisms lesson on reconnection strategies already introduced backoff, jitter, and a maximum attempt count.
That lesson applied those ideas to reconnecting a dropped connection, this lesson applies the same ideas one level up, to retrying individual requests.
The math is identical, only the thing being retried changes, a connection there, a single call here.
If a client is already reconnecting at the transport layer, an in flight request retry usually just waits for that reconnect to finish first.
14. Idempotency Still Matters
Retrying a request that only reads data is almost always safe.
Retrying a request that changes something, like sending a message or charging a payment, can duplicate that action if the client is not careful.

items: Usually safe to retry: reading a resource, listing tools, checking a status.
Needs care before retrying: sending a message, charging a payment, creating a new record.

blocks.text: A retry policy should know which requests are safe to repeat and treat the rest with extra caution.
15. Logging Every Retry
Recording each attempt, its delay, and its outcome turns retry behavior into something visible instead of a hidden detail.
A server that needs constant retries is telling you something worth investigating.
This same logging habit was recommended for reconnections earlier, and it pays off the same way here.
Worked Example
Picture a client calling a tool that looks up a shipping status.
The first call times out, the second call times out again, and the third call succeeds.

code.content:
attempt 1: failed, ETIMEDOUT, waiting about 480ms
attempt 2: failed, ETIMEDOUT, waiting about 1050ms
attempt 3: success

blocks.text: Each wait was longer than the last, and a small jitter kept this client from retrying at exactly the same moment as every other client hitting the same brief outage.
Common Mistakes
A few patterns come up again and again in retry logic that causes more harm than good.

items: Retrying a permission error or a malformed request as if it were transient.
Retrying instantly, over and over, with no backoff at all.
Using backoff without jitter, so many clients still retry in lockstep.
Never setting a maximum attempt count, so a dead server gets retried forever.
Retrying a request that changes data without checking whether it is safe to repeat.
Swallowing the final failure silently instead of surfacing it once the cap is reached.

blocks.text: Practice
Write a retry wrapper around a fake request function that fails four times and succeeds on the fifth.
Give it exponential backoff, jitter, and a maximum of three attempts, then confirm it fails cleanly since three attempts is not enough to reach the fifth try.
Key Takeaway
A good retry policy starts by classifying the failure, retrying a transient network blip and leaving a permission error or a malformed request alone.
Exponential backoff with jitter and a firm maximum attempt count turns that decision into a client that recovers gracefully instead of hammering a struggling server or hanging forever.
